Diakonia
dee-ah-ko-NEE-ah
n. (Greek)
Greek diakonia, “service, ministry, attendance,” from diakonos (servant, attendant; the source of English deacon); possibly from dia- (through) + a root meaning to hasten, the literal sense being running-through in service.

Biblical Definition

Diakonia is the New Testament’s great word for service or ministry—a category that runs across both the most ordinary helping-service in the body of Christ and the most exalted gospel-ministry of the apostles. The Greek word can name the ministry of waiting tables (Acts 6:1, their widows were neglected in the daily ministration (diakonia)), the ministry of the diaconal office (Acts 6:4, where the apostles set apart men for this work that they themselves might give attention to prayer and the ministry of the word), the ministry of giving (2 Cor 8:4, the Macedonian saints’ fellowship of the ministering (diakonia) to the saints), the ministry of the apostolic office (Acts 1:17, 25; 20:24; 21:19; Rom 11:13), the ministry of the new covenant (2 Cor 3:6-9), the ministry of reconciliation (2 Cor 5:18), and the ministry of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:8). The breadth is structural and important. Diakonia in the NT vocabulary covers everything from the most humble physical service to the most exalted gospel-ministry, holding them under one word and thereby insisting that all true Christian work is service. Even Christ Himself is named in this register: even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister (diakonēsai), and to give his life a ransom for many (Matt 20:28—the verb behind minister is the cognate). Two structural points follow. First, the gifts of the Spirit are distributed for diakonia: now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of administrations (diakoniōn, plural of diakonia), but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal (1 Cor 12:4-7); Eph 4:11-12, and he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry (diakonia), for the edifying of the body of Christ. The whole body, by its diverse Spirit-given gifts, exercises diakonia; every saint has a ministry; the church functions when every member is engaged in the service the Spirit has equipped him to render. Second, the diaconal office (servants set apart for particular service in the church, especially to the physical needs of the saints) is one specific application of the broader category. 1 Tim 3:8-13 lays out the qualifications for diakonoi as one of the two NT offices alongside episkopoi (elders/overseers). The deacons are honored, qualified men set apart for service in the church, freeing the elders for the ministry of the Word and prayer (Acts 6) and themselves rendering substantial spiritual ministry through their physical service. The recovery of biblical diakonia is therefore the recovery of the whole-body model of ministry: every saint a servant, every gift given for ministry, the diaconal office held in honor as a real spiritual ministry, and the apostolic-and-pastoral ministry of the Word as the chief but not the only service in the body.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Diakonia: service, ministry, attendance; the NT’s broad word covering everything from the humblest helping-service to the most exalted apostolic gospel-ministry, with the diaconal office as one specific application alongside the wider Spirit-gifted ministry of every saint.

MINISTRY, n. — 1. The act of ministering or serving. 2. Service; agency. 3. Ecclesiastical function; the office or duties of a minister of the gospel. 4. In Scripture, the office of an apostle, prophet, evangelist, pastor, teacher, or deacon, by which the saints are edified and the gospel is preached.

DIAKONIA — (Greek noun, G1248.) Service, ministry. 34 NT uses. Covers physical service (Acts 6:1), diaconal office (Rom 12:7; 1 Tim 3:13), apostolic gospel-ministry (Acts 1:17, 25; 20:24; 21:19), and the ministry of reconciliation (2 Cor 5:18).

Key Scripture

Matthew 20:28 — "Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

Ephesians 4:11-12 — "And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ."

Acts 6:4 — "But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word."

2 Corinthians 5:18 — "And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation."

Modern Corruption

Diakonia-shaped ministry is corrupted, on one side, by the professional-clergy model that has collapsed all biblical ministry into the work of a paid ministerial class and disabled the whole-body ministry the NT assumes—and on the other by the over-democratization that has erased the proper distinctions between the apostolic-pastoral ministry of the Word and the diaconal-and-general ministry of all saints, against the New Testament’s explicit ordering.

expand to see more

The professional-clergy model has, across the post-Reformation centuries and especially in modern Protestant practice, often collapsed all biblical ministry into the work of a paid ministerial class. The pastor is the minister; the laity attend; the saints come on Sunday to receive the ministry of the professional and return to their secular lives without exercising the Spirit-gifted ministry the NT assumes of every member of the body. The result is a passive congregation, an exhausted pastorate (carrying alone what the whole body was given to share), and the loss of the rich New Testament category of diakonia as the active ministry of every saint in the body. The recovery is the recovery of whole-body ministry. Every saint has a gift; every gift is given for diakonia; the perfecting of the saints is for the work of the ministry (Eph 4:12); the pastor’s special work is the equipping of the saints to do the ministry, not the doing of all the ministry himself. The church saturated with this whole-body diakonia is the church the apostles built and the church for which the present passive-clergy-active model is a poor substitute.

The opposite corruption is the over-democratization that has erased the proper distinctions between the apostolic-pastoral ministry of the Word and the diaconal-and-general ministry of all saints. On this account, everyone is equally a minister in every sense; the distinction between elders/overseers (charged with the ministry of the Word, doctrine, discipline) and the wider body (gifted for various ministries of service) is muted; the special qualifications for the office of elder and deacon (1 Tim 3; Tit 1) are treated as optional; the church becomes an undifferentiated body in which no one is particularly responsible for the ministry of the Word and no one is particularly accountable for it. Scripture insists upon both: the wide ministry of every saint (so the whole body is engaged) and the particular ministry of qualified officers (so the Word is faithfully preached, the sacraments rightly administered, the discipline appropriately exercised, the flock rightly shepherded). Recover both. Refuse the professional-clergy collapse that disables the body, and refuse the over-democratization that erases the proper offices. The biblical pattern is whole-body diakonia with ordered officers within it—every saint a minister and qualified men set apart for the particular ministries the NT specifies.

Hebrew Roots

Greek diakonia (service, ministry), cognate with diakonos (servant; the source of deacon); the broad NT word covering everything from the humblest helping-service to the most exalted apostolic gospel-ministry, structured by the whole-body ministry of every Spirit-gifted saint and the particular offices of elder and deacon.

expand to see more

Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry (34 NT uses).

Greek diakonos (G1249) — servant, deacon (30 NT uses).

Greek diakoneō (G1247) — to serve, minister (37 NT uses).

Greek doulos (G1401) — bondservant, slave (the cousin term; emphasizing total ownership rather than service per se).

"The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister—Christ’s own life sets the pattern of diakonia as the shape of Christian service."

"For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry—Eph 4:12 names the equipping of every saint for whole-body diakonia."

"Professional-clergy collapse disables the body; over-democratization erases the offices; biblical pattern is whole-body ministry with ordered officers (elders for the Word, deacons for service) within it."
